messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo, a 35-year-old guitarist whose life had always been a fluid melody of late-night gigs and collaborative studio sessions, now felt trapped in a single, discordant note. Six months had passed since the hit-and-run that had crumpled his van on the way home from a show, but the accident was not over. It lived inside him, a constant, chaotic presence. The event itself was a blur of violence: the blinding glare of headlights in his rearview mirror, the deafening screech of metal on metal, and the sickening lurch as his world spun and then went dark. The other driver never stopped. That fact, the sheer, unanswered injustice of it, was a wound that refused to close.

The memory itself was the first problem. It wasn’t a story he could tell, but a chaotic slideshow of disconnected images: the spiderweb of cracks spreading across his windshield, the smell of gasoline, the specific rhythm of a song on the radio abruptly cut short. When he tried to deliberately piece together what happened, his mind would skid to a halt, unable to form a coherent timeline. These jagged, incomplete pieces left him with the unshakable conviction that his life, the one he had carefully built, had been shattered beyond repair by a random, malicious act for which there was no accountability.

This profound sense of a destroyed life and the burning injustice made him terrified of his own mind. He held a deep-seated fear that if he ever truly confronted the memory, he would unleash a rage so profound he wouldn't be able to control it and would do something terrible. This terror made any deliberate attempt to recall the sequence of events feel not just difficult, but dangerous; his mind would simply go blank, refusing to access the very thing he believed held proof of his ruin. The more he believed his life was over, the more he pushed the memory away, ensuring it remained a collection of threatening, disconnected fragments.

Because the memories came only in these terrifying, unsolicited flashes, he learned that solitude was the enemy. He started to avoid being alone at all costs, filling every potential moment of quiet with chatter and activity to keep the mental slideshow at bay. The belief that he was fundamentally broken and dangerously angry became the organizing principle of his new life. Convinced he could not be trusted alone with his own thoughts, he began to orchestrate a schedule of constant socialising. After band practice, he was always the one to suggest another round of drinks. He’d linger at the studio for hours, inventing reasons to collaborate, anything to avoid the silent drive home and the quiet of his own apartment. He never, ever spoke of the accident, shutting down any attempt by his wife or bandmates to ask how he was really doing.

His relentless campaign of distraction—always staying late, never talking about it, never being alone—had a secondary effect. By refusing to ever sit with the memory, he starved it of the context and narrative that might have rendered it manageable. The fragments remained fragments, disconnected and potent, because he never gave them a chance to become anything else. The strategy designed to protect him from the memory was the very thing that kept the memory toxic and powerful. His life became a frantic effort to outrun his own thoughts, a performance of normalcy that was exhausting him and pushing his wife away. She saw a man who was always surrounded by people but was more alone than ever.

He finally sought therapy after an argument with her. She had pleaded with him to talk to her, to let her in, and in the ensuing silence, he felt a surge of white-hot anger so intense it left him shaking. He didn't yell, but he saw the fear in her eyes, and it terrified him more than anything. It was the moment his fear of his own rage felt most real. He came to his first session not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, convinced his life was already destroyed but willing to try anything to keep from destroying what was left of it himself.
